items.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: Like you have your Holly Hofmann, wonderful flautist here, wonderful

ctx.x: You’ve got to charge up your batteries to keep up with it.

Yeah, man. And you know there are good musicians here you know, but they don’t support it man. Like you have your Holly Hofmann, wonderful flautist here, wonderful, and Charles McPherson, he lives here, Daniel Jackson, he’s here. Who’s the piano player, honey, and the bass player that used to work at Lario’s? Bob Magnusson, and Holly’s piano player.

items.title: Holly Hofmann interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: And Moody’s word of mouth has gotten me a lot of gigs. And he’s been very supportive, very helpful, and as I was mentioning, he often calls me up and plays a lick over the phone for me

ctx.x: Well we were talking about James Moody before I think the cameras were rolling too. He’s quite a personality. Very supportive.

Very supportive. And Moody’s word of mouth has gotten me a lot of gigs. And he’s been very supportive, very helpful, and as I was mentioning, he often calls me up and plays a lick over the phone for me, you know, not so much a lick but a pattern, some interesting pattern with lots of complicated intervals.

He sang a few for us on camera. Here, how about this one? [scats]. Well it’s interesting, he — we shouldn’t be talking about him — but he did say that he mostly learned by ear, it wasn’t until later on that he applied chordal knowledge to what he was already doing. Does that apply at all to how you learned? Or were you learning the theory of improvising along the way?
